# Building the Website

Since this was my first time building a website, I followed the <a href="https://www.marvinschmitt.com/blog/website-tutorial-quarto/">tutorial</a> and template generously shared online by <a href="https://github.com/marvinschmitt/quarto-website-template/">Marvin Schmitt</a>. It gives a step-by-step with helpful explanations that anybody could follow. For the data presentation, I used the Labor and Delivery dashboard template provided by Dr. Zhang in PQHS 431 at CWRU.

I am still in the process of learning R and Github, so I played around with the structures of both templates and Googled function parameters to get an idea of how things work in this environment. Doing so helped me understand the function of each component and become more confident with my coding. With each obstacle, I learned something new.

# Central Hypothesis
**Research question:** How is systolic blood pressure (SBP) associated with sex, education level, and obesity status among U.S. adults?

**Hypothesis:** SBP will vary by sex, education level, and obesity status, with the largest differences expected between obesity groups.

I centered my first project around the hypothesis that higher BMI is associated with higher SBP among U.S. adults between the ages of 21 and 79 years old. I kept it very simple, since the goal of this project is to get comfortable with data presentation on a website using R.

----

# The Data

Data from the NHANES 2017–March 2020 pre-pandemic Demographics, Body Measures, and Blood Pressure Examination files were merged using the unique participant identifier, SEQN. The analytic sample was restricted to participants aged 20–79 years who completed both the interview and MEC examination. Average SBP was calculated from up to three available systolic blood pressure measurements, retaining the mean when at least one measurement was present. Education was collapsed into four categories, sex was coded as female or male, and obesity status was defined using BMI ≥ 30.0 kg/m². Missing values were retained as NA, and participants with complete data on all variables used in the main analyses were identified for quality checks.

----

# Analysis

## Sex vs. SBP

I wanted to tackle the broadest category first, so I chose sex. I found that the mean SBP for females was 121.26 mmHg and for males, it was 126.70 mmHg. The estimated difference in population means (female minus male) was −5.44 mmHg. Then, I used Welch’s two-sample t procedure to obtain the 90% confidence interval for this difference, coming out to −6.16 to −4.72 mmHg. Because interval does not span across 0, the results provide evidence of a difference in mean systolic blood pressure between females and males, with females having a lower mean systolic blood pressure on average.
